question: When the Bank of Canada says it has changed its policy interest rate, which rate is it talking about?
generated_answer:
You may think that when the Bank of Canada lowers or raises its policy interest rate, it affects all borrowing rates equally. You would be right - and you would be wrong. Whether you realize it or not, changes in the Bank of Canada’s policy interest rate have different effects on different borrowing rates over time. Understanding how these changes work can help you manage debt during periods of high and low interest rates. Three interest rates you should know about

There are three interest rates that are important when it comes to household borrowing:

The target for the overnight rate. This is the rate that the Bank of Canada says should be the actual rate at which major banks lend and borrow from one another one-day (or overnight) funds. The target rate is announced by the Bank of Canada eight times a year. It is the basis for other interest rates, including mortgage rates. The prime rate. The prime rate is a rate that banks charge other banks or their most creditworthy business customers. It is influenced by the target rate and is usually the same among major banks in Canada. The prime rate is used to determine variable mortgage rates. Fixed mortgage rates. Fixed mortgage rates are determined by longer-term funding sources and by the demand for five-year mortgage rates. Fixed mortgage rates are not directly affected by changes in the target rate. How the target rate and the prime rate affect your variable mortgage rate

A change in the target rate is the single most important factor for changes in the prime rate. If the target rate rises, the prime rate will also rise. This is true for a decrease in the target rate as well. For example, if the target rate rises by 0.50 of a percentage point from 4.25% to 4.75%, the prime rate will likely rise by the same amount, which means you will pay more in interest on a variable mortgage. This change will take effect right away and will add to your monthly mortgage payment. You can expect changes in the prime rate to be passed on to you by your lender within one to four business days, depending on the lender in question. Most lenders offer a grace period on variable-rate mortgages. This means the increase in your mortgage payment will not take effect for one or two months after your lender has passed on the increase. However, variable-rate mortgages can be renewed at any time, so you may face higher interest costs even during your current term. How the prime rate affects your home equity line of credit

The prime rate also determines the interest you pay on a home equity line of credit. If your home equity line of credit is linked to the prime rate, the lender will charge you interest based on the prime rate charge by your lender. Any increase or decrease in the prime rate will affect the interest you pay. Fixed-rate home equity lines of credit are also available so that you can lock in your interest rate for a fixed period. The interest rate on a fixed-rate home equity line of credit is typically higher than on a variable-rate home equity line of credit because you are protected against a rise in interest rates. The spread between a fixed rate and a variable rate reflects the interest rate outlook for the term as well as the costs of insuring the lender from a rate increase. The prime rate and your credit card interest rate

Most credit cards offered by banks and other financial institutions have a variable interest rate that is affected by changes in the prime rate. You will pay more in interest on a credit card if the prime rate climbs. However, there is a delay before your credit card interest rate will be affected. In addition, if you have a variable interest rate on your credit card, even a small rate increase may impact you because the compound interest effect is working against you. To reduce your costs if the prime rate rises, try to make payments against your credit card balance that are larger than the minimum amount owing. With some lenders, you can choose a fixed-rate credit card. This may protect you against an increase in interest rates for a fixed term, but you must consider the total cost of the loan, including any balance that will remain at the end of the term. A fixed interest rate may be higher than the variable interest rate. The prime rate and your saving rate

Changes in the target rate also affect the interest you earn on your savings. If the target rate rises, your bank may start paying you a higher interest rate on your savings. However, banks usually increase their saving rates more slowly than the increase in the target rate. Your deposit protection

It is important to remember that interest rates affect the value of investments such as Guaranteed Investment Certificates (GICs) and bank term deposits. By knowing the type of investments you have, you will be able to manage your risks. As an investor, you have two key concerns when it comes to your deposits: to receive the interest on your investments and to get your money back when the term ends.
